pages.x: Mexico won its independence from Spain in 1821 and let American settlers into its northern province of Texas. They brought enslaved people, though Mexico had banned slavery, and in 1835 they rebelled. After the fall of the Alamo and a Mexican defeat at San Jacinto, Texas broke away in 1836, and in 1845 the United States took it in.

President James K. Polk believed, like many Americans, that it was their manifest destiny to spread across the continent, and he wanted California. When Mexico would not sell, he sent troops into land both sides claimed. After a clash in April 1846 he told Congress that American blood had been shed on American soil.

Mexico's general Santa Anna, who led the country eleven times, had lost a leg fighting the French in 1838 and buried it with full military honours. At Cerro Gordo in April 1847 he fled so fast that soldiers from Illinois captured his cork leg. It is still in a museum in Springfield, Illinois.

General Winfield Scott landed at Veracruz in 1847 and fought his way inland to Mexico City. In September his troops stormed the castle of Chapultepec. Mexicans remember six young cadets, the Niños Héroes, who died defending it; legend says the last of them wrapped himself in the flag and leapt from the walls.

Many Americans opposed the war as a grab for land that would spread slavery. A young congressman, Abraham Lincoln, demanded to know the exact spot where American blood had been shed, and was mocked as Spotty Lincoln. The writer Henry David Thoreau went to jail rather than pay his taxes, and wrote an essay on civil disobedience.

In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, in February 1848, Mexico accepted the loss of Texas and gave up California, Nevada, Utah and most of Arizona and New Mexico for 15 million dollars. The Mexicans living there became Americans overnight: as their descendants say, they did not cross the border; the border crossed them.

Days before the treaty was signed, a carpenter building a sawmill in California found flakes of gold in the stream. The gold rush that followed brought some 300,000 people in a few years and made California a state by 1850. The fight over whether the new lands would allow slavery helped lead to the Civil War.

The United States reached the Pacific, and Mexico lost about half its land and gained a lasting distrust of its northern neighbour. Ulysses Grant, who fought in it as a young officer, later called it one of the most unjust wars ever waged by a stronger nation against a weaker one.
pts: Mexico gave up about half its land in 1848
The new lands reopened the fight over slavery
